inline.s: So they all came to White Cloud Monastery, where they happened upon Master Qiu Zhenren and a host of fellow cultivators seated in the main courtyard, discoursing on renunciation and the pursuit of the good. Seeing them enter, Qiu Zhenren rose at once and said, "Good fellows, I trust you have been well?" Zhao Bi and the rest no longer recognized Qiu Zhenren. When questioned, they hurriedly replied, "By the protection of the gods we have been kept safe. But where have we met you, master? We have quite forgotten, and beg you to enlighten us." Qiu Zhenren said, "Do you not remember the hungry Daoist on Mount Qinling?" Zhao Bi said, "So you are the master who once instructed us?" Qiu Zhenren said, "If not I, then who?" At these words Zhao Bi and the others all knelt and bowed, saying, "Since we parted more than ten years have passed without our noticing, and we have all grown old and withered. Yet you, master, look younger than before; truly you are a man of the Way! Long ago we said that once you attained the Way we would come to seek refuge with you. We beg you to take us in and receive us as your disciples, pray, what does the master think of it?"
Qiu Zhenren said:

Once, I owed my life to your kindness, and I have not forgotten it to this day. If you say I have attained the Way, in truth I have attained nothing; I merely rely on the Way to awaken the world. Alas! The sea of suffering has no shore; turn your head and the shore is here. In the past I only meant to warn myself, yet who would have thought that upon hearing these words you good fellows would wash your hearts and reform, boldly mending your ways, and so prove yourselves good men. For over ten years you have held your resolve firm. Now you have seen through the red dust and wish to leave the world; this too is a joyful thing.”

But since you have come to leave the world, it is only because in former lives you accumulated good deeds that you could stir up this thought. Though you have resolved to become monks or Daoists, you must scrupulously observe the Dharma's words and precepts. Be compassionate and humble, reverent toward all; do not give way to temper and abandon yourself to your feelings, with a thousand wayward thoughts. All the more should you set aside yourself and follow others; the greatest sin is to harm life. Say not "I am inferior to others" and so give rise to envy. Speak not "he is no match for me" and so breed contempt. Do not use your competitiveness to humiliate others; do not harbor pride (
gong

) that exalts the self. If I am not his equal, it is because my cultivation has not yet matured; if he does not match me, it is because his fortunes have not yet come. The Way has no size, and officers no rank; whether rich or poor, noble or base, what discrimination between high and low, old and young?

He who has the Way is great, he who has virtue is honored. The eager student is like gold and jade; the one who will not learn is like grass and reeds. In this world we prize not gold, silver, or treasure; we value only benevolence, righteousness, and virtue. If the Son of Heaven leaves the world, he is not thereby noble; if a beggar leaves the world, he is not thereby base. In my youth I lost those who upheld me; I was raised to manhood by my elder brother's care. Knowing I had no share in the red dust, I set my heart entirely on seeking the Way and cultivating the truth. Then I met my master, Zhenren Wang Chongyang, who transmitted to me the supreme teaching, and received further from my senior Dharma-brother Ma Danyang deep guidance. After we parted ways at Xie Valley, I pressed myself harder and harder. I suffered great hunger seventy-two times, and more than once was near death; the lesser hungers were countless, and my hardships past telling. Yet my heart was like iron and stone: I would rather die than fall back from my original resolve, and the more trials I endured, the firmer my purpose grew. Later I undertook six years of bitter labor by the Pan Creek, and how can the toil and distress of those years be fully told!

As the saying goes: when bitterness is exhausted, sweetness comes. One day I suddenly awakened, and by Heaven's favor, whenever I prayed for rain, sweet rains fell. For a time my name moved the imperial court, and I was summoned to attend. Though one may say "the fruit of the Way is not yet complete," to reach such a state is no easy thing. Since you wish to leave the world, you should keep this in mind: do not let wealth and rank unsettle your heart, nor poverty and lowliness move your resolve. Regard this body as one already dead, and now as one who has found life within death. Rouse up a great resolve and seek the deathless dharma; only then can you be called a man of supreme attainment.”

When Qiu Zhenren had finished, Zhao Bi and the others all wept and sobbed, grieving over the hardships the master had endured in his cultivation. Qiu Zhenren said, "Unless one reaches the very extremity of suffering, the root of suffering is not exhausted and wisdom is hard to open. I wish you, then, to seek it within suffering. Endure one bout of suffering and one layer of demonic obstacles is dispelled; endure tenfold suffering and all demonic influences are utterly dissolved." When he had finished, he chose a day to don their head-cloths and gather their topknots, and gave each of them a Daoist name, of which we need not speak.

It is also said that the Empress thought to herself: I gave birth clearly to a girl; she was carried out of the hall, and after a turn about she became a boy, and so the great monastery of White Cloud Chan Master was lost to Qiu Changchun. All this trouble has come about because of me alone. Fearing that White Cloud Chan Master would be troubled in heart, she sent a eunuch to summon him to the palace, and consoled him, saying that it was over this little child that the master had been put to such trouble. White Cloud Chan Master said, "The reading was certainly destined to be a phoenix, and I do not know by what heterodox arts Qiu Changchun changed it into a dragon. I fear this is no blessing for the realm." The Empress said, "The Emperor is preoccupied with the lack of an heir, and I dare not speak too deeply on this. Since the sovereign has obtained this child, he reveres Qiu Changchun as an immortal, and every day discusses the Way and expounds the profound within the imperial gardens, seldom returning to the inner palace."

White Cloud Chan Master said, "In the days of Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, the entire court, civil and military, called Zhang Guo an immortal. Xuanzong placed poison in wine and had Zhang Guo drink it. Zhang Guo drank three cups in a row, saying, "There is no good wine, and no good food," then fell into a dazed half-hour, his teeth all turned black. Waking, he hastily demanded the imperial iron ruyi and knocked his black teeth out entirely; closing his mouth for a moment, white teeth grew anew within. Only then did Xuanzong believe him to be a true immortal descended to earth. Now, Matron, why not follow the example of Xuanzong: set a cup of poisoned wine upon the table and summon Changchun to drink it. If he drinks and does not die, then he is a true immortal." When the Empress heard this she was greatly pleased, and at once ordered the eunuch to summon him. How Changchun fared when he came to drink, let us hear the next chapter.
A trick but lightly framed, / even an immortal cannot flee.

blocks.text: 28. The Empress Tests the Way With Poisoned Wine; The Zhenren Wears a Golden Crown and Recites a Verse

inline.s: The elixir's ninefold turning, all pure yang, / transcends the sage and mortal, life long-sustained;
Without one winding course of toil and change, / how could a name through ages be proclaimed?

The story tells that when the Empress heard White Cloud Chan Master's words, she ordered a eunuch to go to White Cloud Monastery and summon Qiu Zhenren, and had poisoned wine prepared beforehand. The eunuch, bearing the Matron's command, went to summon the Zhenren to the palace. The Zhenren already knew her intent; before setting out he instructed Zhao, Li, and the others, saying, "Prepare twenty-four vats of cool, clear water and set them in a single row. When I return I shall have a use for them. Do not fail me, lest my undertaking be undone." Having so charged them, he went with the eunuch into the palace to pay his respects to the imperial consort. The Empress said, "Some time ago the Zhenren calculated that I would surely bear a prince, and so it came to pass. I have no way to repay you, so now I imperially bestow three cups of royal wine as a small token of esteem." At these words she had the eunuch present the wine before the Zhenren. Qiu Zhenren made no refusal and drank off the three cups, then took leave of the Empress and returned to White Cloud Monastery. There he saw the twenty-four vats of clear water ranged along the corridor. He leapt at once into the first vat, and the cold water that soaked him grew hot in an instant. Rising, he leapt into the second vat; when that too grew hot, into the third. In this way he leapt through twenty-three vats. When he reached the twenty-fourth, the water had not been filled to the brim and covered only below his chest. The poison's force was not yet spent; the venomous fire rose, and upon his forehead it scorched away the fine black hair for a breadth of three fingers. Seen from afar, he looked just like the half-bald Daoists of today.

It is further told that White Cloud Chan Master, learning that Qiu Zhenren had not died, entered the palace again to report to the Empress. The Empress said, "If he drank poisoned wine and did not die, he must surely be an immortal." White Cloud Chan Master said, "Or perhaps the wine's poison was too weak to kill, which is possible. I have heard that immortals can subdue the five metals and eight minerals; gold, silver, copper, and iron come to their hands like clay, square when they wish it square, round when they wish it round. The Daoist order has the head-cloth and the crown: the cloth covers the hair, the crown binds it. Now, feigning ignorance, we may call them all by one name, the crown. Let Matron fashion the cloth-and-crown into a golden crown, bestow upon him an ingot of gold, and have him wear it on his head. If it stays fast, he is a genuine immortal. If it will not stay, let everyone laugh at him; he will be ill at ease, without face to meet men, and surely retire to the mountains." At these words the Empress was greatly pleased. She again ordered the eunuch to go to White Cloud Monastery and summon Qiu Zhenren to the palace, and he followed the eunuch to the imperial residence. Seeing that his forehead was bare of hair, the Empress asked, "Why has the Zhenren no hair upon his head?" Unhurried and unruffled, Qiu Zhenren spoke four lines:
Yesterday, by the crimson summons, I climbed jasper stairs, / where the Queen Mother of the West gave me feast and cheer;
Three cups of the wine of long life I drank, / and so opened the gate of heaven at my crown.

When Qiu Zhenren had finished, the Empress felt a pang of shame. She had not wished to test the mystery of the Way again, but she had already agreed to White Cloud Chan Master's plan. So she said with a laugh, "The Zhenren is indeed a true immortal; his divine powers are no small thing and command one's admiration. I have made a golden crown, and the Zhenren may wear it upon his head to complete his noble Daoist bearing." Having spoken, she gave the order. A eunuch brought out an ingot of gold upon an agate platter and said to the Zhenren, "This is the Matron's imperial golden crown; pray, master, put it on that you may render thanks." Qiu Zhenren had long since perceived this, and he carried a steel pin within his sleeve. With both hands he received the gold, and calling up the samadhi fire of true nature, he breathed upon it, whereupon the gold grew soft as clay. Piercing it with his pin, he fixed the ingot upon his hair, and with the pin lifting a few strands, threaded them through the hole. Then, taking up more strands at the point, he bound it front and back. Could that ingot of gold but sit snugly and securely upon his head? The Empress had merely meant, per White Cloud Chan Master's counsel, to make sport of Qiu Zhenren; who would have guessed it would leave a pattern to the Daoist order, for the yellow crowns worn by fellow practitioners today originated right here.
This aside, it is told that Qiu Zhenren, with the gold upon his head, came to thank the Empress, and from his mouth recited a couplet:
Again and again the crimson summons, deep in grace bestowed, / dares I, your servant, recite my verse before the imperial seat;
In the heart of a wise man no hidden sickness lies; / upon a true man's head there is gold that never falls.

When the Zhenren had finished his verse, the Empress grew uneasy, and rising to her feet she said, "I have been at fault! Let the Zhenren forgive me!" Qiu Zhenren said, "What fault is there in the Empress? It is your servant who long clung to the noisy dust and drew his own demonic obstacles." He had not done speaking when White Cloud Chan Master leapt out from behind the screen and, seizing Qiu Zhenren, said, "Qiu Changchun, it was not you who drew these obstacles upon yourself, but I, the old monk, who brought them upon you." Qiu Zhenren said, "The Chan Master is a man to whom the four elements are all empty; how could he cast obstacles upon me? It seems I alone brought this upon myself."
Greedy and lost, clinging to the world's noise, / long in the dust one draws the demon by one's choice;
Affliction comes from my own fault alone, / how can another make my heart to roam?

At that, Qiu Zhenren spoke these four lines and laid the blame upon himself. In truth, White Cloud Chan Master had not been meddlesome; it was the Zhenren who had swapped the dragon for the phoenix and won away his White Cloud Monastery, and so the master gave rise to this small obstruction, urging the Empress to set out wine and bestow a crown in hopes of repayment. If the Zhenren had not taken possession of White Cloud Monastery, how could this dispute have arisen? Therefore the Zhenren's shouldering of the blame was his conscience, which remained unclouded. Later generations should not seize upon this victory and defeat as a matter for idle argument.
Hearing Qiu Zhenren take the fault upon himself, White Cloud Chan Master too repented of his mistaken intent, and offhand spoke four lines:
Having read the sutras, all things are empty he knows, / why then at once did his mind grow dim and raw?
To bandy dragon and phoenix gains nothing at best, / but wastes the heart's contriving in a thankless quest.

The Empress, seeing both the Chan Master and the Zhenren take the blame upon themselves, their wisdom returning as if turning back the light. She was overjoyed, and was about to speak a few words of praise when she heard a palace attendant announce that the imperial carriage was coming. The Empress hastened to welcome the sovereign into the palace, and Qiu Zhenren and White Cloud Chan Master both came to pay their respects. The Yuan ruler was much pleased and said, "I have seen the two masters at odds and have often been anxious. Just now I went to the Western Palace to relieve my spirits when the attendant reported that the two masters had made peace, and my heart was filled with joy. So I left the Western Palace to sit with the two masters in easy talk." The Empress then recounted to Emperor Shun of the Yuan the lines in which the two masters each owned their own fault. The Yuan ruler was delighted, saying that the three teachings are in origin one principle, and monks and Daoists belong to one family. He too wished to say a few words to congratulate the two masters:
One monk, one Daoist in the capital, / monk and Daoist are one family in all;
From this day no need to divide the two, / together we reach the fruit and become a buddha.

Qiu Zhenren and White Cloud Chan Master, hearing these words, thanked the sovereign in unison. Emperor Shun of the Yuan said to White Cloud Chan Master, "I have already disbursed imperial funds for the National Teacher to build a new monastery. When the work is complete, the Buddha images of White Cloud Monastery may be moved into the newly built temple, and a new name taken. Let White Cloud Monastery be transformed into White Cloud Abbey, and the image of the Patriarch of the Way be newly cast, so that monks and Daoists be distinguished, each with its own tradition. Thus for a thousand autumns the incense shall burn, and for ten thousand ages men shall look upon it, never in vain rewarding the two masters' merit in safeguarding the young prince." The Zhenren and the Chan Master again rendered thanks. The Yuan ruler ordered the attendants to set a plain vegetarian feast, and ruler and subjects rejoiced together. During the feast they spoke of the mysteries of the Way and the Dharma of the Buddha: the Buddha set up his teaching on emptiness itself, the Dao took as its foundation the void. Emptiness is naught, and the void is also naught, in the end, it all seems one and the same principle. Before long the feast ended; the two masters took leave of the Yuan ruler and each returned to his own place.

It is also told that the monks who had come out of White Cloud Monastery took up residence in various temples. One day they happened to gather together and deliberated among themselves: "This fine monastery of ours has been taken by Qiu Changchun, are we simply to let the matter rest?" Among them was a monk fond of meddling, who claimed to understand geomancy, and he said, "If you follow my plan, we shall build a West Wind Temple in front of White Cloud Monastery, and I daresay it will work the great defeat of White Cloud Monastery." The other monks asked how such a defeat would come about, and the meddling monk said, "Have you not heard that fengshui fears to be broken? With my west wind blowing away those white clouds, how can I fear defeat, how can I fear they will not scatter?" At these words the monks clapped their hands and laughed, crying, "Marvelous!" At once they made up several subscription registers. Another monk, broad in literary talent, took up his brush and wrote a preface. Together they came to White Cloud Chan Master, begging him to come forward and solicit several official endorsements. Then they told the Chan Master of the plan to blow away the white clouds with a west wind.

White Cloud Chan Master laughed and said, "Who put this plan into your heads?" The monks pointed to the meddlesome one and said, "It is this bodhisattva of a high order." White Cloud Chan Master asked him, "You wish to raise a west wind to scatter the white clouds, what is your meaning?" The monk said, "Your junior wishes to avenge the venerable one." White Cloud Chan Master said, "Since the Buddha established this teaching, we may only form connections of good fortune with others; I have never heard of forming bonds of enmity. Those who leave the world hold the four elements empty and are unstained by a single mote of dust, what enmity is there to avenge? In former times the Buddha, when his body was cut and dismembered joint by joint by King Kali, harbored no resentment, and thereby realized the station of the Great Hero, beyond birth and death. It is wholly through enduring insult with kindness and gentleness that one becomes complete in divine powers. Therefore our school, in its highest teaching, empties all things: no self, no person, without sound or smell. Since there is no view of self or person, what enmity is there to avenge? What wind is there to blow? Moreover, Qiu Zhenren and I have no resentment at all. This White Cloud Monastery was lost by me to him; he did not come and seize it by force. Yesterday the Son of Heaven imperially bestowed funds for a new temple to be built. You have now fabricated these words and stirred up trouble. If the Son of Heaven learns of this and sends down punishment, this old monk cannot bear the weight. If you wish to build it, go and build it yourself." Having spoken, he went off to quiet contemplation.

The monks, hearing White Cloud Chan Master's words, were suddenly awakened, and the plan to raise a west wind and scatter the white clouds dissolved at once. They burned the subscription registers with fire and scattered back to their several temples. Only this monk who claimed to break fengshui was unconvinced at heart; going out he said to this one and that, "I have collected several thousand taels of silver to build a West Wind Temple before White Cloud Monastery. When my west wind rises, it will surely scatter their white clouds, and I will see to it that not one of those Daoists can live there." He thought, by these boasts, to intimidate the fellows of White Cloud Abbey. He little knew that nine out of ten of those Daoists were also fine braggarts. Hearing his words, they too spread rumors abroad, saying, "Let him build, and be done with it. When he has built, we will raise a high wall in front, like a fan. When his wind comes, we will fan it back with one sweep, this is called "returning the wind," and it will scatter itself." Suddenly one man shouted out, "If you can return the wind, then I will go and set fire!" Who was this shouter? Let us hear the next chapter.
Patience and forbearance bring the mind to harmony; / let honor, disgrace, falsehood, truth flow eastward with the stream.

blocks.text: 29. Receiving the Crimson Summons, the Seven Perfected Ones Attain the Fruit; Journeying to the Jade Pond, the Host of Immortals Partakes of the Peach

inline.s: Only when the great Way is cultivated and one leaves the path of delusion / does one count as a true hero among men;
Sharing the light of sun and moon, never decaying, / waxing old with heaven and earth, the Mysterious Capital is made grand.

The story tells that those fellows fond of boasting were just saying, "If he builds the West Wind Temple, we will put up a screen wall outside the abbey. As the old saying goes, "Clouds fear wind, and wind fears a wall." This wall shall serve as a fan; when the wind comes we'll give it one sweep, and the wind will blow back, this is called "returning the wind."" The words were not yet finished when Zhu Jiu, the one who had robbed travellers in the road on Mount Qinling, stood nearby and roared out, "If only you can return the wind, then I will go and set it on fire and burn it clean to the ground!" Seeing him so rash, Wang Neng quickly stopped him, saying, "His temple is not yet built, what will you burn? Wait until he has built it, and then there is no hurry to burn it!" At these words all the fellows burst into laughter.

Who would have thought that some meddlesome Daoist would carry these words abroad and spread idle tales to this one and that. As the years passed, the rumor endured and was handed down untruthfully, until it was taken as fact, the tale running: "A monk built a West Wind Temple to scatter White Cloud Abbey; the Daoists used a counter-spell, returning the wind and turning back the fire, and burned the West Wind Temple down." In truth nothing of the sort happened. It was simply that on one side there arose a meddlesome monk and on the other a boasting Daoist. One said this, the other said that, and it stirred up those fond of provoking trouble, who wove it into a saying. Many old practitioners, born and raised in the capital, could never make heads or tails of the matter. Now, corrected after the old books without error, it may serve so that later followers do not contend over strength and weakness, and so bring luster to the law of cause and effect.
Since ancient days false rumor must not be believed; / told and retold, it grows the more absurd;
Men today take it as real and true, / and ever judge the ancients wrong or right.

It is further told that after Qiu Zhenren had made peace with White Cloud Chan Master, in the intervals of quiet cultivation he likened the practice-work of nine times nine, eighty-one turnings, to the eighty-one hardships of the journey of cultivation. Using true nature and original feeling, the heart-monkey and the mind-horse, as instruments of his own use, and taking the seven emotions, six desires, three corpses, and six thieves as outer demons that seek to seize and plunder, he wrote a great book called Journey to the West. When the book was finished, he sent the acolyte to the Jixian Academy to present it to White Cloud Chan Master. White Cloud Chan Master was a man of great wisdom, and knowing at a glance, he too took the sights of the grotto, the subtle functions within stillness, the six times six, thirty-six roads of outward demons attacking the self, and the transformations whereby wisdom and divine power overcome them, and wrote a great book called Investiture of the Gods; he likewise sent a novice to White Cloud Abbey to present it to Qiu Zhenren. From this time the two families were on good terms. White Cloud Chan Master, now complete in divine powers, flew his staff to the south of the Yangtze to expound the teachings there. This one immortal and one Buddha, having authored Journey to the West and Investiture of the Gods, have left them to endure for ten thousand ages, their subtle uses never exhausted.
In these two great books deep mystery resides; / illusion is made by men, a principle that abides;
Within them the seven emotions and six desires stir, / giving birth to demon kings by the thousand, by the score.

It is further told that Qiu Zhenren established a platform at White Cloud Abbey to preach the teaching, expounded the precepts, and opened wide the door of salvation, reviving the Way of Complete Perfection and setting up rules and standards to warn later generations. He also left behind admonitory writings for posterity, founded the seventy-two great monastic forests of the order, and received descendants of the Mysterious lineage for a hundred thousand years. With three thousand meritorious deeds and eight hundred perfect practices, he was due to answer the call of the Purple Palace and attain the rank of a Great Lofty Immortal.

The thirty-three heavens, the cinnabar writ sends down its decree; on the nineteenth day of the tenth month he rode a crane and ascended. At that time, rainbow light blanketed and refracted, purple vapor soared with true energy, golden boys paired to lead him on, jade maidens in twos to show the way. A gentle breeze stirred, and in mid-heaven banners and pennons danced; clear tones rang bright, and within the clouds celestial music chimed. In an instant he left the land of Beijing, and in a moment came to the Southern Gate of Heaven. The kings Wang, Ma, Yin, and Zhao clasped hands in greeting; Zhang, Ge, Xu, and Sa smiled to welcome him. He paid court to the Sovereign Supreme before the golden hall, and beheld the heavenly countenance in the jade palace. Prostrating himself below the jasper steps, he called himself a subject before the Lingxiao Hall: "Long live our Emperor, without bound! Great is the imperial virtue that cherishes life!" The Most High, seeing him, was overjoyed and ordered an examination of his merits. The Three Officers ascended the hall to recommend the Seven Perfected Ones: "His merit is worthy of praise; weighing his bitter practice in internal and external works, Qiu Changchun is first. Penetrating the subtle mystery of the Ultimateless and the Supreme Ultimate, Liu Changsheng is second. Tan Changzhen, his Dao-mind firm, is ranked third. Ma Danyang, pure and still and non-active, rightly deserves fourth. Hao Taigu, unstained by a single mote, is raised to fifth. Wang Yuyang, with ten thousand thoughts all stilled, should take sixth. Sun Bu'er, her wisdom complete, first championed the practice, and her merit is greatest and should stand above the rest; yet to yield a step, let her, who was first among them, now be last, and take the name seventh, complete from beginning to end. The fruits of the Seven Perfected Ones have already been inscribed in the Purple Palace; now your servant dares to report them." When he had finished, the heavenly countenance was pleased, and one by one it conferred titles upon the Seven: Qiu Changchun was appointed the Celestial Immortal Champion, highest rank of those chosen in the Purple Palace, patriarch of Complete Perfection, the True Lord of Miraculous Manifestation and Resplendent Response, Principal Teacher. Liu Changsheng was conferred the Mysterious and Calm, Virtue-Retaining True Lord. Tan Changzhen the Ancestral-Mystery and Bright-Virtue True Lord. Ma Danyang the Non-Acting, Universal-Transforming True Lord. Hao Taigu the Penetrating-Mystery and Marvellous-Extreme True Lord. Wang Yuyang the Vastly-Compassionate, Universally-Saving True Lord. Sun Bu'er the Mysterious-Void and Harmonious-Transforming Primordial Lady.

When the Most High had bestowed the titles, the six, Liu, Tan, Ma, Hao, Wang, and Sun, all rendered thanks; only Qiu Changchun would not. The Three Officials cried out, "Qiu Changchun, why do you not give thanks?" Prostrate upon the jasper steps, weeping and in fear, Qiu Zhenren replied, "It is not that your servant will not give thanks; it is only that the Way is hard to learn and immortality hard to attain. Among those of later generations who cultivate the Way, who like your servant endure a hundred thousand hardships without retreating from their original resolve, not one in ten thousand is to be found. Learning to be good is the hardest of all; without learning to be good, one cannot complete the Way. Your servant has a memorial, "The Difficulty of Learning the Good," to present:"

To awaken to the Way is not easy; to learn the good is hardest of all. For the learning of the good is a thing that only a person of great strength can undertake. One must be able to endure hunger and cold, to bear insult and disgrace. Sometimes a garment does not last the whole life, and food not last the whole day; one goes without two meals, and at night can scarcely find a single lodging. Not a day passes without drawing men's aversion and contempt, and receiving humiliation again and again, to speak of it is bitter, and to hear it chills the heart.'

"Your servant has passed through a thousand kinds of hardship, and so knows how hard the learning of the good truly is. If this single word "good" is so hard to learn, how could one dare hope for immortality? I fear that the cultivators and seekers of enlightenment of later ages, unable to suffer as I have suffered, will bear the name of seeking the Way without the substance of it. Then your servant would have no means to work their salvation, and would betray the honor of the imperial bestowal; that is why I dare not give thanks. I humbly beg you to pardon my offense."

When Qiu Zhenren presented this "difficulty of learning the good" to the Emperor of Heaven, the host of immortals fell silent. Just then a Star Lord walked out from the Western Great Hall, and do you know what this Star Lord was like?

Born with crimson hair, crimson face, crimson beard, crimson heart; carrying golden helmet, golden armor, golden brick, golden whip; his feet treading three-five fire-wheels, chasing wind and pursuing lightning; commanding a million pixiu (
pixiu

, two kinds of fierce beasts of ancient books, used as a metaphor for valiant warriors), slaying demons and capturing monsters. Impartial in his inspection, men called him the Iron-Faced Thunder Lord; responsive as a protector of the Dharma, all reverenced him as the Primordial Spiritual Ancestor.

The story tells that the Spiritual Ancestor nearby, hearing Qiu Changchun's account of how those who learn the good must endure many hardships with no one to protect them, was moved to compassion, and desired to be a god who protects the Dharma. So he called out in a loud voice, "Qiu Changchun, rest assured and give your thanks. If in later ages there should be cultivators and seekers of the Way, should they maintain three-tenths of practice, I will respond with seven-tenths; should they maintain full practice, I shall shine upon them at all times. There will always be those who prepare alms and make offerings, so that he need not suffer hunger and cold." Hearing the Star Lord's words, Qiu Zhenren at last gave thanks, and conferred his respects upon the Star Lord, laying upon that Star Lord's shoulder a burden of several thousand catties.

After a while the Most High withdrew from the hall and the host of immortals disbanded. The Seven Perfected Ones went together to the Purple Palace to pay their respects to the founding ancestor, the Emperor Lord of Eastern Flower, and to the Patriarchs Zhongli and Lu Dongbin, and also to bow before their master, Zhenren Wang Chongyang. The Emperor Lord of Eastern Flower bade Zhenren Zixia lead the Seven to the Hall of Splendid Ceremony to study the rites of the Jade Pond, so that when the Peach Banquet soon convened they would know how to pay court to the high immortals.

When the day of the banquet came, the Emperor Lord of Eastern Flower led the newly arrived true immortals, the southern and northern schools, the five ministers and seven perfected ones, straight toward the Jade Pond. From afar they saw the towers of jasper, the pavilions of jade, the golden halls and silver palaces, with coral for railings and red jade for stairways. Gold and azure light crossed in splendor; crimson and purple dazzled the eye; auspicious rays met the gaze, and rare fragrance perfumed the air. Within the forests of jade trees and jasper woods, phoenixes flew and sang; beneath golden pillars and silver pedestals, tigers roared and dragons chanted. Dark cranes and plum-deer, blue lions and white elephants, all came matched in pairs. Phoenix-palanquins and dragon-carriages, phoenix-vehicles and crane-mounts, none in the world could rival them. One cannot exhaust the majesty of the Jade Pond, nor fully set forth the beauties of Mount Kunlun.

It is further told that the Emperor Lord of Eastern Flower led the newly arrived host of immortals to pay court to the Queen Mother, who received them with the rites due to honored guests. Before long, sages and perfected ones gathered like clouds, and the Queen Mother received them. When the greetings were done, they took their places according to the ancient custom of former banquets, each in his proper order. Only the newly arrived perfected ones awaited the mistress's arrangement. The Queen Mother of the West said, "The newly arrived immortals, before this supreme sage, cannot each pay respects individually. Let them act according to convenience: stand upon the red steps and bow three times upward, all as one." When the Queen Mother had so commanded, the Emperor Lord of Eastern Flower led the host of immortals to kneel upon the jasper steps, and after the three bows and nine prostrations, they arose.

The Queen Mother settled each in his seat; music of the heavenly harmony resounded, and there was song and dance in rainbow garments. The delicacies on the table were beyond words, none of them belonged to the mortal world. Many immortal lads passed the cups and poured the wine; countless jade maidens held the flasks and raised the ewers. Dozens of boys, carrying baskets of purple bamboo, flew through the air and straight up to the tree tops, plucking the flat-peach from above and filling their baskets and their crates in a moment. Immortal officials and officers passed them on to one another, until in a short while the whole hall was filled with them. The very largest were offered up to the Heaven-Honored Great Sage; those next in size were set before the Great Lofty Golden Immortals and the true spirits of the three realms; those smaller still were awarded to the teaching immortals of the Isle of the Blessed, the attendants and guards, and all their households. These peaches are not easy to eat: only one who has practiced cultivation may obtain them. If followers of later ages long for this peach, let them too, like the Seven, devote heart and will, cultivate the Way and attain the truth, and come reverently to the Jade Pond to bow to the Queen Mother of the West, and the peach will surely be granted to you. Eat one and you live a thousand years, never aging, long-lived and deathless.

When the banquet was over, the thousand perfected ones and ten thousand sages each returned to their heavenly palaces. The Seven Perfected Ones followed the Emperor Lord of Eastern Flower back to the Purple Palace. This Purple Palace is on Mount Fangzhu, which resembles Kunlun but is not so great or high. Within it, too, is grass that stays green through all four seasons and flowers that never fall through the eight festivals; it may be counted the foremost realm of the heavenly palace, yet not easy to reach. A verse says:
The cause-and-effect of the Seven Perfected ever flows, / and we but hope that each of us the mystery knows;
Endure the boundless suffering of this mortal shore, / and become a carefree immortal, and wander no more.
Without nature, life cannot stand; / without life, nature finds no hold;
To cultivate both nature and life is the true key; / buddhas and immortals refine essence and leave the world.
How laughable the foolish, karmic breed, / a wanton skeleton in its stupid pose;
dragging their spirit-nature down to Avici, / this is a blow of the staff to point straight the way

Life is formed of the mother's blood that comes after heaven, and becomes the body. To have a body without nature is like having a house without a person. If there is a house without a person, of what use is the house? Moreover, a person first has nature and then life; just as first there is a person and then a house. With nature and life, one has both a person and a house; with a person and a house, one can accomplish a career. Consider the moment when father and mother unite, it forms a misty blend, and this is called the Ultimateless. The father's passion and the mother's intention, with essence and blood embracing, brings it to be.

The Supreme Ultimate is precisely nature and life, taking form month by month. From the two modes come the four images, and from the four images the eight trigrams. When the embryo reaches ten months complete and falls to the ground with a cry, at the first opening of the mouth nature transforms into the subtle soul, life into the gross soul, and they fall into the organs and viscera of the later-heaven body.

The subtle soul dwells in the liver, the gross soul in the lungs. The liver has three flowers and the lungs seven lobes, so it is said there are three subtle souls and seven gross souls. The seven gross souls are governed by the three subtle souls. The subtle soul loves life and hates death; the gross soul loves death and hates life. Why is this so?

Whenever a person dies, the nature goes to the nether courts, and according to good and evil, merit and fault, is reborn to receive retribution. Born and then dying, dying and then born again, such is the suffering of birth and death. For he who bears the burden of being born, it is like flaying a live ox; for the dead, it is like boiling oil poured upon the heart. Is this not agonizing?

Therefore the subtle soul wishes only for long life without death, to be spared the suffering of birth and death, and escape the calamity of transmigration. The gross soul guards the tomb and craves the offerings. When the subtle soul departs, there is no one to govern the gross soul, and it is left to run loose; hence it delights in death and fears life.

The men and women of the world think only of keeping themselves alive, and know nothing of cultivating nature, how could they understand the work of cultivating both nature and life? They little know that life is the flesh and blood of the later-heaven body, and that nothing is without a principle of decay. Hence it was said before: life is like a house, and nature is like a person. A house long kept must leak, and long leaking must collapse. So if a person can repair the house, he may dwell in it long in peace. If one does not know how to cultivate, by long nourishing the body must decay, and long decaying it must die. Since it was said that nature and life transform into subtle and gross souls, if one does not cultivate, and the soul and gross soul fly apart, is that not a pity?

Master Jigu said, "If a person does not cultivate, it is like a crab put into a pot: though it has seven legs and eight arms, it can find no door by which to escape." Confucius said, "Who can go out without passing by the door?" If one gains the practice of cultivation, refining the three souls and mastering the seven gross souls, so that three and seven unite into one great elixir, then a single beam of spirit-light goes out through the great gate of the right Way, does it not all pass by this one path?

If a person wishes to know the first methods of this practice, he must seek out a true master. With the true transmission and the wondrous secret, refining the soul and governing the gross soul, this is the work of cultivating both nature and life.

The people of the world know only the principle of the forward course, in bearing sons and raising daughters; how could they understand the way of the reverse course, which leads to buddhahood and immortality.

When a person comes from the mother's womb and falls to the ground with his head reversed, the original spirit of the prior heaven transforms into the consciousness-spirit of the later heaven; the original energy of the prior heaven transforms into the breath of the nose and mouth of the later heaven; the original essence of the prior heaven transforms into the copulative essence of the later heaven. This is called the forward course.

Bearing sons and daughters is all a matter of the parents' essence and blood. As the children grow up, the parents must decline, how could they know the meaning of the reverse course that leads to buddhahood and immortality? To understand this meaning, one must seek out an enlightened master to point out the secret of ascending to heaven against the current.

Earlier it was said the prior heaven transforms into the later heaven; now we speak of the later heaven returning to the prior heaven, that is, refining essence into energy, refining energy into spirit, and returning them to the void. This is called the way of the reverse course that leads to buddhahood and immortality.

How pitiable that the people of the world are deluded and will not awaken; the wise go past it, and the foolish fall short of it. They little know that the sages of the three teachings, having completed the Way and ascended to heaven, though they have won freedom, grieve in compassion for the people below. And so they set flowing the scriptures to hand down to the world, wishing to teach later generations to contemplate the meaning within the books. The canonical collection of the sages is clear as though uncovered, and yet the benighted hearts of men regard it as no more than old paper.

The Heart Sutra of the Jade Emperor says, "Recite it ten thousand times, and the marvellous truth will be clear of itself." People today know how to recite but not how to hold it; they recite without holding, which is like reciting in a dream. Therefore the Confucian books say, "Thought without learning is perilous; learning without thought is lost."
The people of the world do not investigate its principle; I now set forth clearly the three teachings, and by the scriptures lead them into the gate of the Way.
